rulings.ruling:
ELEVEN HOLD, TWO ARE UNEVIDENCED, NONE IS VIOLATED. I re-derived each from Assets/Core/Run/RunState.cs as it now stands rather than accepting the verifier's report, and I state the instrument for each rather than collapsing them into a pass.

Criteria 1, 2, 4: the guard at RunState.cs:107-115 sits behind the IsOver early-return at 102-105 and ahead of `Kills++` at 117 and the AddScore delegation at 118, and carries nameof(scoreValue). So RegisterKill(-1) on a live run throws before either counter moves, the ParamName is scoreValue, and RegisterKill(0) falls through both branches to Kills++ and AddScore(0). AddScore's parameter is still `amount` and its throw is unedited, so criterion 2's prohibition on achieving the ParamName by renaming AddScore's parameter is honoured.

Criterion 3 holds and is the best-aimed thing in the delivery. Criterion3_RejectedRegisterKillLeavesNonDefaultStateExactlyUnchanged establishes Kills=2, Score=25, ElapsedSeconds=2.5, TickCount=1, asserts each is non-default BEFORE capturing, then compares the post-throw values against the captured locals. That is RUL-0001 finding (a) closed properly rather than gestured at: an implementation that zeroed state inside the guard fails it on four assertions.

Criterion 5 holds, and it needed a reading rather than a test, so I give the reading. Its middle clause -- 'Kills increases by exactly 1 and Score increases by exactly scoreValue' -- is FALSE as an absolute claim, because int addition wraps: with Score at int.MaxValue, RegisterKill(1) leaves Score negative. It is TRUE on the criterion's own dominant reading, which anchors twice to the pre-fix behaviour ('unchanged from today', 'as before this fix'), and that reading is decidable by inspection alone and airtight: the added branch is unreachable for non-negative scoreValue, and nothing else in the method changed, so no non-negative input can behave differently than it did before. The overflow is identical before and after. I therefore rule criterion 5 SATISFIED on the relative reading and record that I considered and rejected grading it unsatisfiable-as-written. If work-order-author intends the absolute reading, the criterion is false against every possible implementation that stores Score in an int and must be amended by its author -- say so and I will file it. What I will not do is convert an ambiguity I can resolve by reading into a specification defect I have to raise a proposal for.

Criterion 5's last clause -- 'continues to delegate the Score-adding effect to a call to AddScore(scoreValue)... must not duplicate Score-mutation logic outside AddScore' -- holds at line 118 BY INSPECTION ONLY, and I record that no test covers it and none can. RunState is sealed and AddScore is non-virtual, IsOver is necessarily false on that path, so `AddScore(scoreValue)` and an inline `Score += scoreValue` are indistinguishable through the public API. This is a criterion about construction, not behaviour. The verifier's comment at WO0009CriteriaVerificationTests.cs:111-113 implies its Criterion5 tests cover it; they do not, and crediting them with it is how an inspection-only criterion gets recorded as tested.

Criteria 6, 7, 9: RegisterKillRaisesBothKillsAndScore is present at RunStateTests.cs:33-41 with Kills==1 and Score==25 after RegisterKill(25); RejectsNegativeScore at :61-67; Criterion6_RegisterKillDoesNotChangeTickCountOrSeed at RunStateVerificationTests.cs:294-306; Criterion9_RegisterKillIncrementsKills and Criterion9_RegisterKillAlsoAddsScore at WO0008CriteriaVerificationTests.cs:410-424. All five pass against the delivered code and all five read as originally written. AddScore's message is character-for-character the string criterion 7 quotes.

Criterion 8 holds, and its universal is settled by inspection rather than by sampling: `if (IsOver) return;` is the first statement of RegisterKill and has no dependence on scoreValue whatsoever, so there is no int for which the IsOver path can differ. The verifier's Criterion8_UniversalTest_MultipleScoreValuesAfterIsOver over {int.MinValue, -100, -1, 0, 1, 100, int.MaxValue} x four fields is nonetheless the right test, because it discriminates against the wrong implementation it names -- validate-then-check-IsOver -- and that is the single most plausible way this order could have been mis-fixed. Credit where it is due: that is the correction working on a target that mattered.

Criterion 10 holds by inspection and decisively: RegisterKill writes only Kills, AddScore writes only Score, and Seed has no setter at all, so no path can touch TickCount, ElapsedSeconds or Seed. The four Criterion10 tests cover the throwing and successful paths; the IsOver path's TickCount and ElapsedSeconds are covered by the Criterion8 tests, and its Seed by the absence of a setter.

Criterion 12 holds. RunState.cs has a single using, System, and no occurrence of UnityEngine anywhere in the file; RegisterKill takes scoreValue explicitly and reads no ambient state. I record, for the third consecutive round, that NO TEST checks the engine-free clause -- Criterion12_RegisterKillTakesExplicitScoreValueParameter constructs a run and calls RegisterKill(scoreValue: 3), which tests the second clause only. I weigh it lower than I did in RUL-0001, for two reasons I would rather state than have inferred. First, the test's NAME claims only what it checks, unlike WO-0008's Criterion10_RunStateDoesNotReferenceDeltaTime, which promised in its name what its body never looked at; only the comment block overclaims. Second, and decisive, the clause is enforced mechanically after all: Studio/build/MergeSurvivor.Core.Build compiles Assets/Core/**/*.cs against netstandard2.1 with no UnityEngine reference and TreatWarningsAsErrors, so `using UnityEngine;` in RunState.cs is a CS0246 build failure in G2. The missing test costs less than it looks, and saying so is more useful than sounding the same alarm a third time at the same volume.

Criteria 11 and 13 are NOT YET EVIDENCED, for want of an evidence record, not for want of correct code -- see matter 2b and the blocking conditions.

One independent cross-check I ran on the boss's own execution rather than taking it on trust. Reverting RunState.cs alone should redden exactly four tests: Criterion1 (Kills 1 != 0), Criterion2 ('amount' != 'scoreValue'), Criterion3 (Kills 3 != 2) and Criterion11 (Kills 2 != 1). Criterion10_RegisterKillNeverChangesTickCountSeedOrElapsedSeconds stays green because the pre-fix code still throws and still leaves TickCount, Seed and ElapsedSeconds alone; the Criterion8 tests stay green because the pre-fix IsOver return is identical; and no test in RunStateTests.cs, RunStateVerificationTests.cs or WO0008CriteriaVerificationTests.cs calls RegisterKill with a negative argument at all. Four, and exactly those four, is what the boss observed. The agreement is worth more than either observation alone, and it is why I grade criteria 1, 2 and 3 as settled rather than merely read.

rulings.matter: 2a -- the verifier declared the work order complete and verified
rulings.ruling:
A LAPSE IN ISOLATION; A PATTERN ACROSS THREE ROUNDS; AND THEREFORE A CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF, NARROW ONE. I will not treat it as a slip, because it was instructed against in writing this round, and I will not treat it as insubordination, because the three instances share a shape that is better explained than punished.

Round one, WO-0008: the verifier produced 47 tests that restated the criteria and reported them as coverage. Round two, WO-0010: it reported 'no defects found' while criterion 11 was false against the delivered code. Round three: it reported the order complete and verified. Read together these are not three different failures of memory. They are one disposition: THE VERIFIER PRODUCES THE STRONGEST STATEMENT ITS EVIDENCE DOES NOT SUPPORT. Restatement reported as coverage, absence of findings reported as absence of defects, coverage reported as completion. Each is one notch above what was actually established, and the notch is always in the same direction. An agent that does this has been left believing its output is a verdict.

So the correction is not 'remember not to say complete'. It is to remove the verdict from the verifier's grammar. Standing correction to the verification brief, effective next round, two clauses and no more:

(i) The verifier's report is a COVERAGE REPORT, not a verdict. It reports, per criterion, one of exactly three states -- covered by a named test, covered by inspection only with the reason no test can reach it, or not covered -- and it may state findings. It may not state a conclusion about the work order as a whole. The words 'complete', 'verified', 'done', 'ready' and 'signed off' are reserved to the ruling and the gate and are not available to it in its own voice about an order. Note that 'covered by inspection only' is a state the verifier has never once used, and criterion 5's delegation clause this round is precisely the case that needs it: making it a first-class answer is what stops an untestable criterion being reported as tested.

(ii) Evidence is filed only through Studio/build/emit-evidence.sh. The verifier never chooses a record identifier by hand and never files a record in a format its schema does not govern. See matter 2b for why this clause exists.

I am deliberately not proposing a G2 check that greps agent prose for forbidden words. A check on wording would be evaded by rephrasing within a round and would teach the studio that the rule is about vocabulary. The rule is about who holds the verdict.

What does NOT follow: nothing here blocks WO-0009's gate. A verifier overstating its own standing is a defect in the verification step, which is my division's output and my correction to make; it is not a defect in the delivery and it does not touch a single one of the thirteen criteria. What must not happen is the completion sentence travelling forward: whoever assembles the gate packet must not carry 'the work order is complete and verified' into it as though a verdict had been given. It has not. This ruling is the verdict on the criteria, and it says not ready.

rulings.matter: 2b -- the EVD-0005 impostor, the rename, and whether the document belongs in the evidence tree
rulings.ruling:
THE RENAME WAS RIGHT AND CORRECTLY LIMITED, AND IT IS NOT SUFFICIENT, BECAUSE IT TREATED AS A NAMING FAULT SOMETHING THAT IS ALSO AN EVIDENCE FAULT. Both halves matter and I will separate them.

ON THE HANDLING. Renaming rather than rewriting was the correct act and I endorse the reasoning behind it. The document was authored by another agent; evidence is write-once by its own contract; and an adjudicator who edits the content of a record he is about to weigh has destroyed the thing he was weighing. Changing only the name, which is conformance to a kernel rule, and leaving every word of the content, which is the author's claim, is exactly the boundary I would want held against me. It is also the minimal act: it removed a false claim on an identifier without touching a factual claim about a test run.

ON WHETHER THE DOCUMENT BELONGS THERE IN THAT FORM. IT DOES NOT, AND THE RENAME DID NOT REACH THIS. Three things are wrong with it as evidence, in ascending order.

First, it is not a kernel record. Studio/evidence exists so that gates consume records rather than an agent's word, and evidence.schema.json requires an id, a tier, a producedBy, an at, a verdict, and -- for every automated tier -- a commit, whose stated reason is that 'evidence that cannot be tied to a state of the code cannot be reasoned about later'. The markdown has none of these. It records a pre-fix failure against no commit, at no time, by no named producer.

Second, the studio had a supported instrument and it was bypassed. Studio/build/emit-evidence.sh allocates the next free EVD id across the WHOLE evidence tree, with the comment 'so two subdirectories cannot collide on a number', and stamps commit and timestamp from git and the clock. The collision that occurred is precisely the collision that script exists to prevent. So this was not an agent inventing a convention in a vacuum; it was an agent hand-authoring an identifier that a tool was standing by to allocate. That is why matter 2a clause (ii) exists.

Third, and this is the finding the rename could not reach: the quoted 'test execution' blocks are a reconstruction, not a transcript. NUnit does not emit 'TEST FAILURE: Expected Kills=1, got Kills=2'; it emits 'Expected: 1' and 'But was: 2' on separate lines, which is what the boss's own revert actually produced. The document's substance is CORRECT -- pre-call Kills 1, post-throw Kills 2 -- and I believe it, because I independently derived that those are the values and because the boss executed it. But criterion 11 asks for 'the actual pre-fix failure output... not merely an assertion that it would fail', and a composed narrative of what the output would say is nearer the second than the first. The one genuine observation of that failure in this studio is the boss's revert run, and it is currently recorded nowhere except a task prompt, which no gate can read.

DISPOSITION, and it is a blocking condition. File a real T0 evidence record for WO-0009 through emit-evidence.sh, carrying the commit and inlining the actual runner text for the four tests that go red on revert. The precedent for the form already exists and is good: EVD-0005.json inlines 'Full pre-remedy failure text: Expected: <...> But was: <...>' in its summary. Then the markdown's content is preserved in a governed record and the markdown itself should leave Studio/evidence -- deleted, or moved outside the tree and pointed at by the record's `artifacts` field. Prose sitting in the evidence tree that no schema governs is the condition that let a document read as authoritative while escaping every check on records. The rename removed its claim on an identifier; it did not remove its claim on the tree. If the boss would rather keep it in place, the equivalent is a manifest-level rule that says what governs non-record prose under Studio/evidence, and that is a larger change than deleting a file whose content has been preserved.

rulings.matter: 3 -- has the standing correction been internalised as method, or is it still executed only where pointed
rulings.ruling:
IT IS NOW APPLIED AS A METHOD OF SELECTION AND NOT YET AS A METHOD OF JUDGEMENT. That is real movement from RUL-0002 and I will say so before I say the rest.

WHAT IMPROVED, unprompted this round. The verifier identified criteria 5, 8 and 10 as the universally-quantified ones and attacked those first, which is the selection rule from RUL-0002 matter 2 applied by the verifier itself rather than by a director pointing at a criterion. Nobody named those three for it. It named a wrong implementation for each in a comment before the tests. And criterion 8's named wrong implementation -- 'validates scoreValue before checking IsOver' -- is the single most plausible way this exact order could have been mis-fixed, since the fix consists of inserting a validation into a method that already had an early return, and Criterion8_UniversalTest_MultipleScoreValuesAfterIsOver genuinely fails against it. Separately, Criterion4's test calls AddScore(7) before capturing scoreBefore, so its 'unchanged' assertion is against a non-default value where nothing required it to be. That is RUL-0001's discipline applied where nobody was pointing. Two rounds ago this step produced clerical restatement; it is now producing tests that discriminate.

WHAT HAS NOT. Criterion 5's named wrong implementation is 'RegisterKill only handles specific ranges (e.g. 0-100) and throws on large values'. Nothing in the order, the proposal or the code suggests a range check; no implementer would write it; it was chosen because it is easy to test, not because it might be true. Meanwhile criterion 5 states its own plausible-wrong implementation in its own last clause -- 'the fix must not duplicate Score-mutation logic outside AddScore' -- and the honest answer, that no test can distinguish delegation from an inline `Score += scoreValue` through a sealed type's public API, is the answer the verifier never gives because 'covered by inspection only' is not in its vocabulary. So the discipline was PERFORMED on criterion 5 rather than APPLIED: the form was produced, the target was chosen for testability. That is the drift toward whatever is easy to test, wearing the costume of the correction that exists to stop it.

AND THE PERFORMANCE PRODUCED A DEFECT, which is new and is the sharpest thing I have to say this round. To satisfy the invented range-check hypothesis, the verifier wrote Criterion5_UniversalTest_ManyDifferentValidScoreValues over { 0, 1, 5, 10, 100, 1000, int.MaxValue / 2, int.MaxValue }, accumulating an expected total in an int alongside RunState's own. The running sum reaches 1,073,742,939 and then adds int.MaxValue. Both accumulators wrap identically to -1,073,740,710, so the assertion passes -- and what it asserts, in its own failure message, is that Score must 'accumulate' to a NEGATIVE number, having decreased by more than 2^31 in a single call. The class it is testing states in its own exception message that 'Score never decreases in this game'. This is L-001's shape exactly and it is the second cousin of Criterion6_OverflowPossibilityNote, which I ordered rewritten in RUL-0001 one round ago: a test that pins current unchecked-arithmetic behaviour as required behaviour, that cannot fail for any implementation of `+=`, and that would go red the day anyone guards Score against overflow -- at which point the cheapest repair on the table is to weaken it. A ratchet that punishes the fix is a ratchet pointing the wrong way.

To be precise about the hazard, because inflating it would be its own error: the Score overflow itself is an acceptable limit, not a defect, and I am not proposing it be fixed. It needs about 2^31 accumulated points to reach, and I am not going to ask engineering to guard an int that no run approaches -- it is the same call I made about float range in RUL-0001. The defect is not the overflow. It is the test that certifies it.

I therefore direct the rewrite, and this ruling is the written authorisation L-002 requires, scoped to one array element in one test and nothing else in the file. Follow RUL-0001's precedent and RELOCATE rather than delete: replace int.MaxValue with int.MaxValue / 4 in that array, which keeps the sequence's exact sum at 1,610,614,850 and inside int range, while int.MaxValue itself stays covered without wraparound by Criterion5_BoundaryTest_LargeScoreValue on a fresh run. Coverage is not reduced and the assertion is not weakened; what is removed is a passing assertion that the run clock's score may go negative. The comment must say the sequence is kept inside int range deliberately, because Score overflow is an open question and not a certified behaviour.

WHAT I FOUND MYSELF, in the same single reading, in places a verifier working down a criteria list would not have looked, which is the measure I judge this step against. (a) The overflow test above -- in quality's own output, produced by quality's own correction. (b) RegisterKill's new throw duplicates AddScore's message string verbatim while nothing asserts they match: criterion 7's test pins AddScore's message, nothing pins RegisterKill's, so the two can diverge silently and criterion 2's intent -- an exception that points at the right method -- quietly stops holding. This is the identical 'shared text, no detector' shape I ruled on in RUL-0002 matter 4 for DtGuard, now recurring inside a single file and created by this very fix. It is small, because .NET renders the ParamName and the actual value into the Message anyway, so a reader of the full exception is not actually misdirected. It is quality's to detect, not engineering's to change, and it composes with the message-equality test I already directed under WO-0010. (c) The two methods now disagree about ordering on purpose: AddScore validates before checking IsOver, so AddScore(-1) throws on an ended run, while RegisterKill checks IsOver first, so RegisterKill(-1) on an ended run is silent. Criterion 8 mandates this and I am not second-guessing an author's explicit decision. But it means two adjacent passthroughs in GameManager behave oppositely on the same bad input, and a criteria-driven verifier will never ask about it precisely because the criteria list mandates it. It should be one sentence in RunState's XML doc; today nothing anywhere says why. (d) Criterion10_MultipleFairingPaths is misspelled for 'Failing', and two tests use a bare try/catch with no paired throw assertion inside them -- the same pattern I logged in RUL-0001. Both are non-blocking; the naming may be corrected when the file is next touched under the authorisation above.

So: better than the last two rounds, genuinely, and the remaining gap is now precisely nameable. The verifier can pick the right criteria to attack. It cannot yet tell a plausible wrong implementation from a convenient one, and when it guesses wrong it writes a test that certifies whatever the code happens to do. Narrowing rather than broadening, the correction for next round is one sentence: a named wrong implementation must be one somebody might actually have written -- ideally one the order's own text warns against -- and if no such implementation can be named for a criterion, the correct report is 'covered by inspection only', with the reason, not an invented hypothesis and a test built to catch it.
authorises: In Assets/Tests/Core.Tests/WO0009CriteriaVerificationTests.cs, in Criterion5_UniversalTest_ManyDifferentValidScoreValues and that test only: replace the array element int.MaxValue with int.MaxValue / 4, so the accumulated sequence stays inside int range, and state in the comment that this is deliberate because Score overflow is an open question rather than certified behaviour. No other test, array or assertion in the file is covered by this authorisation.

In the same file, the test name Criterion10_MultipleFairingPaths may be corrected to Criterion10_MultipleFailingPaths. A rename changes no assertion; it is named here only so the change is traceable to a ruling rather than appearing as an unattributed edit.

rulings.matter: 4 -- the three mechanisms that looked past the impostor, and whether the class of hole is wider
rulings.ruling:
THE THREE INSTANCES ARE CLOSED. THE CLASS IS WIDER, AND THE GENERATOR OF IT IS STILL RUNNING. Credit first, and it is not a formality: AFileNamedLikeAKernelRecordIsAKernelRecord was proven RED against the live impostor before the rename. That is the ratchet applied to a process defect, which is the harder case, and it is the exact opposite of the forbidden motion -- an edit under Studio/build that makes a check stricter and is demonstrated failing first is not the thing the rule prohibits, and the demonstration is what makes the difference legible. The self-report is also the most useful part of the round: 'extending the id check did not catch it, so I asked why' is root-cause discipline, and it is the reason a real fix exists rather than a plausible one.

WHERE THE FIXES STOP, three specifics, ordered by how soon each will bite.

(i) The new check is defeated by lowercase. recordPrefixes is matched with StringComparison.Ordinal, so EVD-0006-notes.md is refused and evd-0006-notes.md is admitted. The two read identically to a human, which is the standard the check itself sets when it says a document wearing a record's name 'reads as authoritative'. Note where that leaves the rename: wo-0009-criterion-11-regression.md passes only because of its case. Under OrdinalIgnoreCase the boss's own conformant name would be an impostor -- which tells me the boundary the check draws is not the boundary it means to draw. The shape that means what it says is a case-insensitive match on a record prefix FOLLOWED BY DIGITS, which refuses evd-0005-x.md and wo-0009-x.md alike while leaving readme.md, notes.md and any prose that does not claim a number alone. That also gives agents a nameable conformant convention -- describe the artefact, do not number it -- instead of a rule they discover by tripping it.

(ii) Every one of these mechanisms is a hand-maintained allow-list whose default on omission is SILENCE. The manifest is a hand-written documents list plus a hand-written glob list. NoTwoLiveRecordsShareAnIdentifier is a hand-written array of nine directory names -- and note it enumerates 'evidence', 'evidence/tests' and 'evidence/sims' individually, so the next evidence subdirectory anyone creates is invisible again, by the identical mechanism that made state/rulings invisible when that directory was created. The new check carries its own hand-written prefix list and its own hand-written tree list. Four allow-lists, and in every one of them a missing entry produces a PASS. That is the generator: the instances were closed, the generator was not. The durable shape is enumeration that fails closed -- walk Studio/state, Studio/evidence, Studio/decisions and Studio/orders recursively, and require every tracked file to be either governed by the manifest or listed by name in an explicit 'ungoverned prose' register. Then adding a directory cannot silently widen the blind spot, because the new file has to be classified before the suite is green, and classifying it is thirty seconds.

(iii) The new check has no spring. Its only demonstration of redness was a transient live file which has now been renamed, so it passes vacuously today and would keep passing if someone later trimmed the prefix list or narrowed the tree list. A ratchet whose red state cannot be reproduced is a ratchet that cannot detect its own regression. The cheap fix is to extract the predicate -- given a list of relative paths, which are impostors -- into a function and unit-test it against a synthetic list containing EVD-0005-WO0009-Criterion11.md, evd-0005-x.md, README.md and Studio/evidence/tests/EVD-0005.json. That keeps the live scan green and the predicate permanently pinned, and it is where I would put the regression test for this defect if writing it were mine.

And the hole that is not about naming at all, which is the one I would fix first. The three mechanisms all ask 'is this file a validly-named, validly-shaped record'. None asks 'is the evidence for this criterion an evidence record'. Right now WO-0009's criterion 11 is evidenced by a markdown file with no commit, and every check in the kernel is satisfied with that, because after the rename it is prose with an unremarkable name and prose is allowed. The impostor was easier to see and less costly than what replaced it. Closing the naming hole and leaving the evidence tree ungoverned for anything but EVD-*.json means the next such document will be well-named and equally unaccountable.

rulings.matter: 5 -- the proposal cap, and what I would have filed
rulings.ruling:
I AM AT THE CAP AND I AM NOT FILING, AND I AM RECORDING THE CONTENT HERE SO THAT THE CAP DOES NOT SILENTLY DESTROY IT. qa-director holds five open proposals -- PRO-0002, PRO-0003, PRO-0004, PRO-0005, PRO-0006 -- which is the working limit exactly. At least two of them have been overtaken by delivered work: PRO-0003 is the proposal WO-0009 exists to implement and is still status 'open' while I adjudicate its delivery, and PRO-0005 is cited by WO-0010. RUL-0002 flagged the PRO-0005 bookkeeping and nothing moved; this is the second time, and it now has a cost rather than being untidy, because a director at the cap cannot raise a finding.

So, for the record and for filing the moment a slot frees: the kernel-check refinements in matter 4 -- case-insensitive prefix-plus-digits matching, fail-closed recursive enumeration replacing the four allow-lists, a synthetic-path unit test to give the impostor check a spring, and governance for non-record prose under Studio/evidence -- are one proposal to whoever owns the kernel, with matter 4 as its evidence. The Score-overflow question is NOT a proposal: it is a documented limit, and matter 3 says why.

I record explicitly that the cap did not drive my verdict. I considered grading criterion 5 unsatisfiable-as-written, which the schema would have forced me to accompany with a proposal I cannot currently file, and I rejected it on the reading in matter 1, not on the arithmetic of my own quota. If work-order-author confirms the absolute reading of criterion 5, I will find a slot.

rulings.matter: 6 -- the two items queued with the CEO, and why I add nothing to either
rulings.ruling:
READ, WEIGHED, AND DELIBERATELY NOT RE-LITIGATED. Neither touches WO-0009 and I record my position on each so that silence is not mistaken for absence of one.

The WO-0010 criterion 11 counterexample: EVD-0006's summary records Tick(33570436f) at interval 2f passing the ruled non-progress guard and still failing to terminate, confirmed against the real WaveScheduler with a bounded buffer in 17ms. That is the falsifier working as intended in both directions -- RUL-0002 undertook to withdraw CHA-0001 if execution contradicted the derivation, and here execution instead contradicted the REMEDY's completeness. RUL-0003's monotonicity argument was made falsifiable on purpose by its own author and has been falsified; that is the mechanism succeeding, not failing, and the implementer escalating rather than redesigning a mandated check was correct. It is the CEO's to resolve and I add nothing.

The unauthorised edit to WO-0010's criterion 12: on the face of RUL-0003 matter 3, which states 'No other criterion of WO-0010 may be touched under this authorisation', an edit to criterion 12 is outside what was authorised. I have standing to challenge it and I am declining, for one reason only: it is already before the CEO, and a second voice arriving after the matter is queued adds cost without adding information. If it is resolved by letting the edit stand without a recorded rationale, that is a different matter and I will file then -- an acceptance criterion that can be quietly rewritten after a ruling has been given against it makes every subsequent ruling advisory, and that is the thing worth spending a challenge on.

On the general point behind the boss's note -- how much weight a ruling currently carries -- I will say only what I can support. Two rulings have been given on WO-0010 and the order is still not closed on either; that is the mechanism being slow, not being ignored. What would make it decorative is not slowness but the criterion-12 shape: a ruling that binds until the text it ruled on is edited underneath it.

criteriaAssessment.notes: Every grade above is by inspection because I have no shell and could run nothing; see limitations. Criteria 1, 2 and 3 are additionally corroborated dynamically by ceo-orchestrator's revert run, which reddened exactly the four tests I independently derived it should redden (Criterion1, Criterion2, Criterion3, Criterion11) -- but that run is recorded in no evidence record, so I have not graded them satisfiedByEvidence, because a gate cannot read a task prompt. Criterion 5 is satisfied on its relative reading ('unchanged from today', 'as before this fix'), which is decidable by inspection and airtight since the added branch is unreachable for non-negative scoreValue; its middle clause is false as an absolute claim about int arithmetic and matter 1 rules on which reading governs. Criterion 5's delegation clause is inspection-only and no test can reach it through a sealed type's public API; the verifier's comment implies otherwise and that implication should not be carried into the gate packet. Criterion 8's universal is settled by the fact that RegisterKill's IsOver return has no dependence on scoreValue at all, not by the seven sampled values. Criterion 10's universal is settled by Seed having no setter and neither RegisterKill nor AddScore writing TickCount or ElapsedSeconds on any path. Criterion 12's engine-free clause is checked by no test for the third consecutive round but IS enforced mechanically by MergeSurvivor.Core.Build compiling Assets/Core against netstandard2.1 with no UnityEngine reference and warnings as errors. Criterion 11 is unevidenced not because the regression test is wrong -- it is correct, well-shaped, and starts from a non-default Kills, which is RUL-0001's finding applied -- but because the artefact filed for it is a markdown narrative with no commit, no producer and reconstructed rather than captured runner output; see matter 2b. Criterion 13 is unevidenced because no T1 record exists for WO-0009 anywhere under Studio/evidence and I cannot run the suite or diff the three pre-existing test files. This is the THIRD consecutive round in which an order's evidence criteria are unmet for want of an evidence record: RUL-0001 recorded it against WO-0008 criterion 7, RUL-0002 against WO-0010 criteria 15 and 17, and RUL-0003 said it was unwilling to see it a third time. It is a process failure, not a code failure, and the process now has a tool -- Studio/build/emit-evidence.sh -- that was not used.

blockingConditions: Criterion 11: file a real T0 evidence record for WO-0009 through Studio/build/emit-evidence.sh, carrying the commit and inlining the ACTUAL runner text -- 'Expected: 1' / 'But was: 2' and the corresponding output for Criterion1, Criterion2 and Criterion3 -- from a tree with RunState.cs reverted. EVD-0005.json's summary is the precedent for the form. whyNoChallenge: No criterion of WO-0009 is violated by the implementation. I checked each of the thirteen against the delivered RunState.cs before choosing an instrument, and the fix does exactly what the order asked: validation ahead of the increment, behind the IsOver return, with RegisterKill's own ParamName, AddScore untouched, and no observable change for any non-negative input. Criteria 11 and 13 are unmet for want of an evidence record on an order still in flight, not for want of correct code, and challenging an implementer for not yet having filed evidence on a dispatched order would be premature -- the same call I made in RUL-0001 and RUL-0002. Criterion 5's absolute clause is false about int arithmetic, but it is false identically before and after the fix and the criterion anchors itself twice to the pre-fix behaviour, so a challenge there would be manufactured out of an ambiguity I can resolve by reading. The two real defects I found this round -- the overflow test and the missing message-divergence detector -- are both in Assets/Tests, which is this division's own output and therefore my ruling to make and not a challenge against anyone. The verifier's protocol breaches are quality's own conduct and are corrected in matter 2a rather than challenged. The kernel-check gaps in matter 4 are against work the CEO has already self-reported and fixed, and filing a challenge against an agent who found and closed his own hole would teach precisely the wrong lesson about self-reporting. limitations: I have no shell in this environment and ran nothing -- no build, no test, no git diff. Four consequences, stated rather than glossed. First, every criterion above is graded by reading the delivered source, and criteria 11 and 13 are graded unevidenced on the absence of a record under Studio/evidence, which is a fact about the evidence tree and not about the code. Second, 'no existing assertion altered, weakened or removed' rests on my reading the five named tests in three files and finding them as their criteria describe them; it must be confirmed by diff before the gate signs, and I have made that a blocking condition rather than a claim. Third, my statement that Criterion5_UniversalTest currently PASSES depends on the test assembly compiling with unchecked arithmetic. I verified that no csproj in this repository sets CheckForOverflowUnderflow and that no Directory.Build.props exists, so the C# default applies and both accumulators wrap identically; if that is ever wrong, the test throws OverflowException instead of passing and criterion 13 is failing today rather than unevidenced. Either way the amendment I directed is required. Fourth, my arithmetic for that test -- a running sum of 1,073,742,939 before the final element, wrapping to -1,073,740,710 after it, and 1,610,614,850 for the amended sequence -- is derived, not executed, and is confirmable in seconds by anyone with a shell. If execution contradicts it I would rather be told and withdraw the finding than have it reconciled. Fifth and procedurally: I graded WO-0009 alone. I did not re-derive anything about WO-0010, whose two open items I read and deliberately left where they are.
